elements.quote: Effectiveness of Non-Pharmacological Interventions for Treating Post-Stroke Depressive Symptoms: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
elements.reason: The title explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review and meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Objective: To compare the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a clear objective statement.

elements.quote: Study Selection: We included randomized controlled trials comparing non-pharmacological interventions to control conditions for depressive symptoms in people following stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the inclusion criteria (RCTs, non-pharmacological interventions vs control, post-stroke depressive symptoms).

elements.quote: Data Sources: A literature search was performed through the following databases from January 2000 to August 2018: MEDLINE; CINAHL Plus; Scopus; Academic Search Complete; Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials; Scopus; and Library, Information Science and Technology Abstracts.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources but fails to report when the search was last performed (it only gives a range of years for the studies included, not the date the search was conducted).
The abstract does not mention the methods used to assess risk of bias in the included studies.

elements.quote: Data Synthesis: Thirteen non-pharmacological interventions were categorized into four types... Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention... and at follow-up...
elements.reason: The abstract describes the synthesis methods (categorization and meta-analysis).

elements.quote: Of 1703 identified articles, 22 trials were included in narrative synthesis, of which 13 were eligible for meta-analysis. ... Thirteen non-pharmacological interventions were categorized into four types: complementary and alternative therapy (five trials, 228 participants), exercise (four trials, 263 participants), psychosocial therapy (two trials, 216 participants), and multifactorial therapy (two trials, 358 participants).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies and participants, and summarizes characteristics.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract reports results for the main outcomes.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract reports summary estimates and confidence intervals for the meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect (negative effect size indicates beneficial effect of NPIs over control).
The abstract does not summarize limitations of the included evidence.

elements.quote: Conclusions: Non-pharmacological interventions can be effective in addressing depressive symptoms in people after stroke. Complementary and alternative therapy and psychosocial therapy appear to be promising strategies for improving post-stroke depressive symptoms. Future studies are required to identify a personalized approach for people with specific conditions such as cognitive impairment.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of the results and implications.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide a registration name or number.

elements.quote: Prevalence of major depression in people after stroke is 25% at the acute stage and 31% at 3 months poststroke 2 ; however, few individuals receive effective management for depressive symptoms post-stroke. 3 Unaddressed depressive symptoms can lead to devastating effects... Previous studies have been conducted to identify appropriate interventions for post-stroke depression; two common types are pharmacological interventions and non-pharmacological interventions (NPIs). 5-9 Three meta-analyses have been conducted to provide synthesized evidence on the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions for depressive symptoms following stroke, but results were mixed. 5,6,9... With mixed conclusions, the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions for post-stroke depressive symptoms has not yet been determined.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge regarding post-stroke depression and the mixed results/uncertainties surrounding pharmacological interventions.

elements.quote: Moreover, it is recognized that the application of pharmacological interventions might be further limited due to adverse effects, long response times, potential medication adverse events, and low adherence rates. 8,10,11 For these reasons, an alternative, or addition, to pharmaceutical options is essential to ensure effective management of depressive symptoms after stroke. NPIs, which are defined as science-based and non-invasive interventions on human health, may provide an alternative to ameliorate depressive symptoms.
elements.reason: The text explains the limitations of current pharmacological treatments and the need for exploring non-pharmacological interventions (NPIs) as an alternative, establishing the need for the review.

elements.quote: Three reviews have identified several NPIs for post-stroke depression and have qualitatively provided evidence. 8,11,14 In particular, the latest review indicated that therapies demonstrating a reduction in depressive symptoms include problem-solving therapy, acupuncture, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, music therapy, exercise, light therapy, motivational interviewing, and robotic-assisted therapy. 8 However, none of these reviews quantitatively demonstrated the effectiveness of different types of NPIs. Therefore, to address this research gap, this study aimed to conduct a meta-analysis to synthesize and compare the available evidence regarding the effectiveness of various NPIs for treating depression in people following stroke.
elements.reason: The authors identify existing qualitative reviews on NPIs and explain that the current review is needed because previous reviews did not quantitatively demonstrate the effectiveness of these interventions.

elements.quote: NPIs, which are defined as science-based and non-invasive interventions on human health, may provide an alternative to ameliorate depressive symptoms. Several NPIs for depression exist, such as complementary and alternative therapy (CAT), exercise, psychosocial therapy, non-invasive cranial stimulation, and multifactorial behavioral treatment.
elements.reason: The text briefly describes the nature of the interventions (NPIs) being reviewed.
The review does not utilize a logic model, and it is not a requirement to create one unless the authors choose to do so for complex interventions.

elements.quote: Objective: To compare the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the objective of the review.

elements.quote: The PICOS (Participants, Interventions, Comparisons, Outcomes, Study Designs) checklist was used to identify the inclusion criteria in this review. 17 Participants (P): This review included trials if they targeted persons with stroke... Interventions (I) and controls (C): This review considered trials that compared the effects of NPIs for post-stroke individuals with depressive symptoms... to control conditions, such as usual treatment. Outcomes (O): The primary outcome of this review was depressive symptoms... Study designs (S): This review considered any RCT...
elements.reason: The review explicitly defines the planned comparisons and scope using the PICOS framework.

elements.quote: The PICOS (Participants, Interventions, Comparisons, Outcomes, Study Designs) checklist was used to identify the inclusion criteria in this review. 17 Participants (P): This review included trials if they targeted persons with stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic), regardless of comorbidities and any previous treatments, but excluded those with manic or psychotic episodes/symptoms... Interventions (I) and controls (C): This review considered trials that compared the effects of NPIs for post-stroke individuals with depressive symptoms... Outcomes (O): The primary outcome of this review was depressive symptoms, measured by any validated depression scale. Study designs (S): This review considered any RCT with a pre-post design, meaning that outcomes were measured at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and follow-up.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly defines the inclusion criteria using the PICOS framework, covering participants, interventions, comparisons, outcomes, and study designs.

elements.quote: The search was restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) written in English and published in peer-reviewed journals.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies language (English) and publication status (peer-reviewed journals) as eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: Of 22 included trials, we excluded three trials indicating publication bias and six trials reporting insufficient data. Reasons for insufficient data were: (1) authors of three trials did not respond to emails for the requested information, 28-30 (2) authors of one trial refused to provide data, 31 (3) authors from one trial did not keep the data, 26 and (4) authors of one trial did not have the requested information. 32
elements.reason: The review distinguishes between exclusion due to publication bias (outcomes not measured/reported in a way suitable for meta-analysis) and exclusion due to insufficient data (results not reported/available), providing specific reasons for the latter.
